sources.title: NGSS 3-LS1-1: Develop models to describe that organisms have unique and diverse life cycles
Monarch Joint Venture: Monarch life cycle
University of Maryland Extension: Metamorphosis life stages of the monarch butterfly

legend.name: Chrysalis
legend.meaning: Jade green with a gold band

steps.title: Milkweed leaf
steps.instruction: Trace the milkweed leaf. A monarch's life starts here.

note.text: Monarchs lay their eggs only on milkweed, because it's the only plant their caterpillars can eat.
The vein carries water into the leaf and food out of it, keeping the leaf alive for the caterpillar to eat.

steps.title: Egg
steps.instruction: Trace the tiny egg on the leaf.

note.text: Stage 1. A monarch lays one egg at a time on the underside of a leaf. After 3 to 5 days, a caterpillar hatches.
note.remember: An egg is about the size of a pinhead.

steps.title: Egg ridges
steps.instruction: Draw the ridges on the egg's shell.

note.text: Monarch eggs have fine ridges running down the shell, like a tiny lemon.

steps.title: Caterpillar
steps.instruction: Trace the caterpillar's body and head.

note.text: Stage 2, the larva. It eats milkweed nonstop and grows about 2,000 times heavier in two weeks.

steps.title: Body segments
steps.instruction: Draw the lines between the body segments.

note.text: Its body is made of segments, which let it bend and stretch. It grows in five stages, shedding its skin each time it outgrows it.

steps.title: Chrysalis
steps.instruction: Trace the twig and the chrysalis hanging from it.

note.text: Stage 3, the pupa. Inside, the caterpillar's body breaks down and rebuilds into a butterfly over 1 to 2 weeks.
note.remember: Butterflies make a chrysalis; moths spin a cocoon.

steps.title: Gold band
steps.instruction: Draw the gold dots near the top of the chrysalis.

note.text: A monarch chrysalis has a row of shiny gold dots. Scientists still study what they're for.

steps.title: Wings
steps.instruction: Trace all four wings of the adult butterfly.

note.text: Stage 4, the adult. Two pairs of wings let it fly far to find food, mates and places to lay eggs.
note.remember: Adults reproduce, so the cycle starts again.

note.text: Like all insects, an adult butterfly has three body parts: head, thorax and abdomen. The wings attach to the thorax.
Antennae help the butterfly smell and keep its balance while flying.

steps.title: The cycle
steps.instruction: Draw the arrows from stage to stage, going clockwise.

note.text: The arrows make a loop: an adult lays eggs, and the cycle starts again. This change in body form is called metamorphosis.
note.remember: Egg, larva, pupa, adult: complete metamorphosis.

steps.title: Color
steps.instruction: These are a monarch's real colors, simplified. The caterpillar stays white because its stripes are too fine to fill.

steps.title: Stage order
steps.instruction: Tap the stages in order, starting from the egg.
steps.why: A caterpillar hatches from the egg, forms a chrysalis, and comes out as an adult that lays new eggs.
steps.hint: What hatches out of the egg?

steps.title: Label the stages
steps.instruction: Pick the right name for each numbered stage.

targets.role: Laid on milkweed; hatches in about 4 days.
Eats and grows, shedding its skin as it gets bigger.

mistakes.Pupa: The pupa doesn't move or eat. This stage is busy eating: it's the larva.

targets.role: The body is rebuilt into an adult inside the chrysalis.

mistakes.Cocoon: Moths spin cocoons. A butterfly pupa is a chrysalis, made from its own hardened skin.

targets.role: Flies, feeds on nectar, and lays eggs.

commonMistakes.Nymph: Nymphs are young insects that look like small adults, like grasshoppers. Butterflies change completely instead.

steps.title: Explain
steps.question: Why does a caterpillar eat so much?

options.text: To store energy for growing and changing into a butterfly
options.feedback: Yes. The pupa doesn't eat at all, so the larva must store all the energy it needs to rebuild its body.
Adult butterflies do eat: they sip nectar from flowers through a long tongue.
The chrysalis's color comes from the pupa's own skin, not from what it ate.
Caterpillars can't fly at all. Wings only form inside the chrysalis.
